doc.title: Jerome Richardson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 9, 1996

title: Soprano sax on Quincy Jones records and his LP collection
summary: Rowe praises his soprano playing on Walking in Space; he recalls Manteca and the idea of playing it in six, then talks about moving LPs and offering them to the archive.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Well Quincy must have been fond of your playing, because I have here one of his great records, and —
“Gula Matari” or something?
This is “Walking in Space.”
Oh, yeah.
And I have to say that the soprano sax that you played on this one tune here, “I Never Told You,” was just gorgeous. Do you remember that recording?
No.
Well it was great.
I remember one time I did Dizzy Gillespie playing [scats].
Oh, yes, “Manteca?”

“Manteca.” And I played a soprano solo in the middle. And they were trying to decide how they would play it, and I told Quince I said, “Why don’t you do it in six?” So he did it in six, and then put strings behind it. So it sounded good. Even I have to say so.
Yeah. Well that’s a beautiful record. And your soprano playing is gorgeous. Roland Kirk.
“I Never Told You So.” Do you know how it goes?
It features Toots Thielmans on the harmonica.
Yeah, but I wonder, I can’t remember how it went.
[scats] I can’t really sing it. But there’s a spot in the middle where you do a really lovely soprano sax. Trust me. You should listen to it.
Yeah, I’ve got a lot of LPs I’ve got to get rid of. Since I moved back here I moved all my stuff from Los Angeles, and I had a whole house full of stuff. I’ve got about six boxes.
Well you know, the Hamilton College Jazz Archive would be glad to talk to you about taking your albums.
Really?
Yes. We can talk about that later if you want.
Well what I was trying to do, what I was hoping to do is sell them to people who would take them.
Well we’ll talk about that too. We’ll talk.
Okay.
